blocks.x: And little Lester Allen, that comedian that was with White Scandals, he was there. All kinds of big people in show business. They were all at that party that night. I can't remember all of them.
Because theater treasures had a close contact with them.

That's right. The legit theaters. They were all there, and Joe Frisco went nuts about our band. He didn't even dance. All he did all night long from the time we started to play, he just sat on a chair right in front of the bandstand and went out of his noodle about this band. A lot of the others did too, Sophie Tucker, all of them. They thought they were really paying attention to that band.
Joe Frisco, it was always a real stutter with him, wasn't it?
Yeah, that was never put on. That was perfectly natural and normal.
Well, I told you, if we jazz enthusiasts wanted to look for a patron saint, it would be Joe Frisco,
I said. That's right. Yeah. You're not missing the mark much there, I'll tell you that.
He was certainly an early man to appreciate what a jazz band could do for an act.
Yeah.
Because for his dance, he needed a great band.

Well, I tell you, he heard this Browns band from Dixieland in New Orleans, and he come back to Chicago to Smiley Corbett's Cafe there, the Lamb's Cafe, raving about this Browns band from Dixieland. And he kept on raving and kept on raving until Smiley Corbett finally gave up and had the band come up. And Corbett was still of the old school, pretty much. He thought they ought to be playing dinner music at night, you know. Boy, what a joke that is. Yeah. So, the full band didn't play the dinner music. The red brown switch from trombone to guitar, and there was a string bass, and Gus Miller playing clarinet. Yeah. And I went down to hear them play. I heard so much about a jazz band, and I had never heard a jazz band in my life and didn't know what jazz sounded like. And this was the summer of 1915, about July around there. I went down there one night to have dinner before going out to the Sheridan Inn at Broadway and Devon where I worked at night. And here were these three guys, and I thought, well, gee whiz, this is not so hot. Where's the rest of the band, huh? And you know what they started to play for dinner music? This guitar, string bass, and clarinet, black and white rag, strictly Dixieland style. Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.
A little softer, though.
Oh, no. Uh-uh. No.
No.
And, boy, was that comical. And I never did get to hear that whole band either, because that was the only time of the night I could get down there. They weren't in Chicago very long.
They left and went to New York for a week or two.

The Browns band, well, I tell you, they eventually split up. Uh, Waddy Wasworth, who was in that, uh, College Inn band, it was Waddy that landed that job at the College Inn in 1915, February. They had never had dancing at the College Inn before. Strictly an orchestra, straight legit orchestra that, in between skating shows, they just sat there and played a concert, a semi-concert number once in a while.
It was in the basement. In the College Inn.

In the College Inn. And they had an ice skating rink there for the performers. So, Walter Blaufus had the orchestra down there for the skating show and everything. And when he heard that they were going to put in a dance band, he went to the union and kept them from coming in. He kept them from, uh, so that they couldn't join the union. He fixed it up. Oh, yeah, I see. I see. So, uh, the Sherman House said, okay, you can get out and they can, they'll come in anyhow. Well, when Walter was about to lose the job down there and they were going to cut out the ice skating show, then Walter, after trying, like, all get out to keep them from joining the union, he went over there and fought with his fingernails almost, I guess, to, to get them into the union. And he, they got into the union and they went down there and started to play for dancing. And they alternated between the skating shows and dancing.
This is Wadsworth.

Waddy Wadsworth landed the job, the saxophone player, who had had the band at the Winter Garden that I told you about. And, uh, so, Bert Kelly was a pretty smart guy. And he, he said to the boys as they were getting there at the end of the week, he said, gee, he says, uh, here are the four of us. We are here. We got the job. We ought to have somebody that could talk to the boss. And Bert says, I'll talk to him. He, he's the one that brought it up. And he also said, I'll talk to him. If that's all right. They said, okay. So he not only talked to the boss, but when it was time for them to get paid, they got paychecks signed by Bert Kelly.
You mean the boss would pay Bert and then Bert split it up?
That's right. It was Bert Kelly's job. He finagled and it was his job.
Well, Bert had gotten in with, uh, Wadsworth then.

Wadsworth was the guy that, uh, really booked the job and landed the job and hired Kelly as the banjo player. So from then on, uh, uh, Kelly, and it was, I guess it was Erking Wadsworth pretty much. And they, if Wadsworth probably was out of there and that's when Kelly got Gus Miller to come in to play clarinet and tenor saxophone. And he, uh, Gus. And the band had broken up. And that's what broke up the band. Uh, Ray Lopez, uh, went with another band over at the, uh, Windcliff Inn. I told you about that too, I think. It was in the basement of the Windsor Clifton Hotel where, that's where Carson Perry's Cotton Company's men's store is now. And Benny Fields and Benny Davis and Jack Salisbury were a singing trio in the Windcliff Inn. And, uh, Ray Lopez was, uh, in the band. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Salisbury were a singing trio in the Windcliffe Inn, and Ray Lopez was in the band that played for dancing down there. And Ray Lopez's father was the clarinet player. He could play the New Orleans style clarinet fairly well, you know, nothing to brag about. Ray Lopez, yeah. And Charlie Thorpe played piano there for the singers, and Earl, what the heck was his name, Earl Chigrew or some such name as that, played piano with the dance band. And then later on when Benny Fields married Blossom Sealy, Ray Lopez went with that act and played in the pit for where...
That's how they got... Well, what do you say about Ray Lopez being the best of the early Dixieland trumpet players is supported by, say, Frankie Quartel, for example. He swears by Lopez.
Yeah, I like Lopez. One thing that made me think that Ray Maxson was from New Orleans... I think he's a great guy. He might have. I'm pretty sure he... I thought they were a team, Fred. I think he's
from New Orleans. I'm pretty sure that he worked in New Orleans before... before he ever came to Chicago. But... Maxson could shoot the bull something awful... also. So...
To be very truthful with you, I never cared much for him. .
Who do you remember from the New Orleans gang playing at Shields Impresso?

Well, yes, I liked Shields playing and Rapoli with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, or Rapolo or whatever his name was. He was all right, too. And of course, Johnny Dodds with Joe Oliver. Oh, Jesus. He was great. I thought he was wonderful.
Did you ever hear Jimmy known him?

Yes, very good. I was trying to think of his name just last night, I think. He had a style of clarinet playing that was very, very nice, very soft and subdued, but very nice clarinet playing. He used to work at the old Apex Club on 35th Street. Yes, he was a very nice clarinet player. Yes. He was a clarinet player. But I'll say this. We'll get back to Johnny Dodds again. That guy was strictly a New Orleans jazz clarinet player, but brother, his instrument always sounded like a clarinet. Yeah. Always sounded like a clarinet and a good, fine clarinet tone, too. Those Teschmarkers and all the rest of those guys, you can have them. I'll take Johnny Dodds every time. And this clarinet player that's with Al Hurt, oh, he's very good. The little bell. Yeah, that little shrimp. Very good man on a clarinet. Oh, brother, he can get plenty of stuff out of a clarinet. Oh, he really gets it out. There are five very exceptional men in that outfit. But when they're all playing, it's like five individuals playing, not like a group sounding like one organized group. It sounds like five individuals, each playing individually. And they're all great performers. But when they're all playing at the same time, they should fit in together and they don't. Each one is an outstanding performer, really performing, but performing by himself with no, just going on, you know.
Well, you said that Louie and Oliver performed pretty much by themselves. That's right, the same way. How does it sound like an integrated band? And by integrated, I just mean it was.
Yeah. No, those bands in those days sounded pretty rough and, you know, there should have been just a little bit of refinement about the sound.
They weren't arranged.

They were totally lacking in the way of an organized sound, you know, and just a little touch of refinement or a little touch of know-how in regarding to playing as a group. And that's what Al Hertz Band needs. They need to learn how to play as a group, not as individuals. But as individuals, brother, there's about five of them that are great. And of course, that takes in Al Hertz. Al Hertz and that clarinet player and the, oh, the drummer that he's got. He's tremendous, man. He is some drummer, that guy. Wonderful.
You talked about Vic Burton as having supported the band. Oh, yeah. He's a great drummer. Do you remember anybody else impressed you that way in your experiences?
Well, there were other good drummers. Herb Quigley, for instance.
The preceding have been excerpts from an interview of George Jug Jernberg, a trumpet player around Chicago for the 20s and into the 30s. The interviewer was John Steiner.
